Editorial rewrite of advisor and client prose; substance unchanged.

advisor.summary: Section 163(j) limits the business interest deduction to business interest income plus 30% of adjusted taxable income; whatever is disallowed carries forward indefinitely. OBBBA resolved the largest open variable: ATI is once again EBITDA-based — depreciation, amortization, and depletion add back — and permanently so, restoring genuine headroom for capital-intensive borrowers. Two structural exits remain: the §448(c) small-business exemption ($32 million average gross receipts for 2026, tested with aggregation) and the irrevocable electing-real-property-trade-or-business election, which buys unlimited interest at the cost of ADS lives and forfeited bonus on the trade's real property. The engine does not compute the limitation — this record exists so that no leveraged client's plan promises interest deductions Form 8990 would take back.
mechanics: Under §163(j)(1), business interest expense is deductible up to business interest income plus 30% of adjusted taxable income (plus floor-plan financing interest); the disallowed balance carries forward indefinitely under §163(j)(2), and a partnership's excess interest passes out to its partners, deductible only against future excess taxable income from that same partnership.

Post-OBBBA, adjusted taxable income under §163(j)(8) excludes depreciation, amortization, and depletion — P.L. 119-21 made the EBITDA-style add-back permanent for tax years beginning after 2024 — so heavy first-year cost recovery no longer shrinks the interest ceiling.

The §163(j)(3) small-business exemption lifts the limitation for taxpayers passing the §448(c) gross-receipts test — a three-year average of $32 million or less for 2026 — but §448(c)(2) aggregates commonly controlled entities, so a group cannot escape the ceiling by splitting receipts.

A syndicate is a tax shelter no matter how small: an entity that allocates more than 35 percent of a loss year's losses to limited owners forfeits the small-business exemption under §448(d)(3) — a trap that springs precisely when leveraged businesses post losses.

A real property trade or business may elect out irrevocably under §163(j)(7)(B); the toll is ADS depreciation under §168(g) — longer lives, straight line, no bonus — on its nonresidential real, residential rental, and qualified improvement property, permanently devaluing future cost-segregation work.

Form 8990 houses the computation at the entity level; the working levers are debt placement across aggregated entities, income timing to release partner-level carryforwards, and re-testing the receipts ceiling before every financing decision.

authority.note: The statutory core: the 30%-of-ATI ceiling and the indefinite carryforward of disallowed business interest.
ATI is once again computed without depreciation, amortization, or depletion — the permanent EBITDA base that lifts the ceiling for capital-intensive borrowers.
The small-business exemption and the aggregated gross-receipts test that guards it — a $32 million three-year average for 2026, indexed annually.
The syndicate definition: allocating more than 35% of losses to limited owners creates a tax shelter barred from the exemption.
The electing real property trade or business exit and the ADS depreciation it imposes on the trade's real property.
The definitions and the C corporation and partnership mechanics that the Form 8990 workpapers implement.
Where the limitation is actually computed and every carryforward is tracked.

requirements: Material business interest expense — leveraged real estate, equipment-heavy operations, or acquisition debt large enough that the 30% ceiling matters.
Gross receipts computed under the §448(c) aggregation rules and re-tested each year against the indexed ceiling.
For the real-property election: a qualifying trade plus a modeled comparison of freed interest against ADS lives and forfeited bonus over the hold period.
Form 8990 workpapers maintained for every entity carrying interest expense.
risks: The real-property election is irrevocable: electing out to fix one bad year permanently surrenders bonus depreciation and cost-segregation value on the trade's real property — the most expensive cure for a temporary problem.
Syndicate status in a loss year strips the small-business exemption regardless of receipts; screen loss allocations to passive members before anyone relies on being under $32 million.
Partner-level carryforwards release only against excess taxable income from the same partnership and can sit stranded indefinitely.
Growth or an acquisition can push aggregated receipts over the ceiling mid-plan, converting expected deductions into carryforwards — a cash-flow surprise arriving in the year leverage peaks.

There is no leading litigation battleground here because the limitation is mechanical — the exposure is preparation failure (no Form 8990, missed aggregation, an unscreened syndicate), all of it self-inflicted.
stateNotes: Conformity: state treatment of §163(j) is genuinely mixed — several states decouple from the federal limitation or compute it on a separate-entity basis, so a binding federal limitation does not automatically carry to the state line; confirm every state in the client's footprint.

PTET interaction: an entity-level PTET deduction lowers entity income and with it adjusted taxable income, shrinking the §163(j) ceiling — sequence the PTET election only after confirming interest headroom.

Missouri: conforms to the federal limitation through rolling IRC conformity (RSMo §143.091), so Form 8990 results flow into the Missouri starting point; the Missouri SALT Parity Act election (RSMo §143.436) is the PTET whose ATI effect is flagged above.
reviewChecklist: Aggregated three-year average gross receipts computed and documented against the 2026 ceiling of $32 million.
Syndicate screen completed for every loss-year entity with passive or limited owners.
Where the limitation binds: Form 8990 prepared and the carryforward's release path identified before any savings are presented.
Any real-property election modeled over the full hold period (freed interest vs. ADS and lost bonus) and its irrevocability acknowledged by the client in writing.
No modeled strategy in this plan assumes an interest deduction the limitation would disallow.

client.teaser: Past a certain size, loan interest stops being an automatic write-off — we keep yours deductible.
client.headline: Keep the interest on your business debt fully deductible
plainEnglish: Most owners assume loan interest is always a write-off. Above a certain size, the tax law caps it. The cap is tied to a share of what you earn each year. Interest over the cap gets pushed into future years instead of helping you now.

There are ways out. Businesses under about $32 million in sales are exempt, counting related companies together. Real estate businesses can make a one-time choice that removes the cap for good. That choice has a real cost, so it needs careful math first.

Our job is to check whether the cap touches you before you borrow. If it could, we measure how much interest is at risk and plan around it. Nothing here changes how you run the business — it protects deductions you were already counting on.
client.analogy: Think of a height limit on a parking garage. Most cars never notice it. If you drive something tall, you want to know the clearance before you pull in.
benefits: Confirms your interest write-offs are safe before you sign new debt
Keeps smaller companies inside the full exemption
For real estate: a permanent way out, tested with real numbers first
No surprises in a down year, when the cap bites hardest
steps: WE measure your sales against the exemption line, counting related companies the way the IRS does.
WE compute how much interest is at risk if the cap applies.
WE model the real estate choice both ways before anything is signed.
YOU loop us in before major new borrowing so the plan stays current.
clientCommitments: Tell us before taking on major new debt or buying another company
Share year-end financials for each related company so the sales test is accurate

annualMaintenance: Re-test aggregated gross receipts against the indexed ceiling every year
Screen loss-year allocations for syndicate status before relying on the exemption
Refresh the Form 8990 computation and carryforward schedule alongside the return
deliverables: Gross-receipts aggregation workpaper documenting the annual exemption test
Form 8990 computation and carryforward schedule wherever the limitation binds
Election memo modeling any real-property trade election over the hold period
